documents.unit: Office of the Dean of Students
documents.title: Guidance on Preventing and Identifying Unauthorized Artificial Intelligence Usage
documents.summary: Faculty-facing guide from the Dean of Students tied to the Honor Code Charter. It advises clear syllabus and assignment AI statements and gives tips for identifying and handling suspected unauthorized AI use, with cautions on detectors and an educative tone. It does not itself say which AI uses are allowed.
documents.stance_why: The page says work must be 'of their own creation' and urges a 'syllabus statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions regarding the usage of artificial intelligence', leaving permissions to each instructor and stating no college-wide allowed or banned uses; so it delegates.

units.why: Quotes the Honor Code Charter that work 'is expected to be of their own creation'; this is a student-ownership expectation (P29), stated as a rule for students, so actor student, modality must, general phase.
units.anchor: all work that students submit is expected to be of their own creation
units.frag_start: According to the Honor Code Charter

units.why: The purpose sentence says the guide 'is meant to guide faculty on both preventing unauthorized artificial intelligence usage and identifying' it, which sets the scope and purpose of the guidance (P56 rather than a definition type P61).
units.anchor: guide faculty on both preventing unauthorized artificial intelligence usage and identifying

units.why: States the rationale that 'It is essential for students to develop and submit their own work' to meet curriculum goals; a learning rationale, so P41 (skill-building) rather than P29 which is the ownership rule itself.
units.anchor: It is essential for students to develop and submit their own work
units.fit_note: Rationale is about meeting curricular goals by submitting own work, not explicitly about practice building skill.

units.why: Says easier access to AI tools may be used 'whether intentionally or inadvertently' to submit work not the student's own; context-setting problem statement, informs. No type fits a background statement that misuse may be inadvertent, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: whether intentionally or inadvertently, to develop and submit work that is not students’ own
units.frag_start: At the same time, access to generative
units.uncovered_note: States that AI misuse may be intentional or inadvertent as background to the guidance, without setting a rule.

units.why: 'Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions regarding the usage of artificial intelligence' is a directive to instructors to put an AI statement in every syllabus: P09; worded 'ensure', coded must.
units.anchor: Ensure that your syllabus contains a statement relating to the Honor Code and permissions

units.why: Points faculty to sample syllabus statements by discipline; a resource for writing the statement, so it belongs with P09 communication rather than P04 (who decides).
units.anchor: has collected sample syllabi statements for Generative AI tools by discipline
units.fit_note: Offers sample statements as a resource rather than requiring one.

units.why: 'Going beyond the syllabus statement' by discussing AI misuse implications at the start of the course is about explaining the rules and ethics to students (P66), advice with 'can help', so should.
units.anchor: discussing the implications of AI misuse in the subject and potential career fields
units.frag_start: At the beginning of your course

units.why: 'Going beyond the syllabus statement when it comes to ethics and artificial intelligence can be beneficial' recommends dialogue with students beyond the written rule: P66 (explain and discuss), should.
units.anchor: Going beyond the syllabus statement when it comes to ethics and artificial intelligence

units.why: 'Assignment prompts ... should include specific parameters for AI usage' tells instructors to state AI rules in assignment instructions, matching P09 ('syllabus or assignment instructions').
units.anchor: should include specific parameters for AI usage

units.why: Adds that specific prompts 'can help deter and detect unauthorized tool use', a rationale for assignment-level AI parameters; coded P35 because the assignment wording is designed to deter and detect, not just communicate.
units.anchor: Specific prompts can help deter and detect unauthorized tool use
units.fit_note: Assignment wording is used as a deterrent and detection aid; no grading or structure change.

units.why: States that under the revised Honor Code faculty 'are now permitted, but not required, to proctor in-person examinations'; a permission for instructors tied to exams. P33 is nearest (unassisted assessment) but the passage is about proctoring being optional.
units.anchor: faculty are now permitted, but not required, to proctor in-person examinations
units.frag_start: Under the revised Honor Code charter
units.fit_note: Proctoring is optional for faculty rather than a required shift of weight to proctored assessment.

units.why: Says a supportive faculty presence at exams 'can help serve as a resource to students ... and deter academic integrity issues'; rationale for proctoring, informs, P33 as above.
units.anchor: A supportive faculty presence can help serve as a resource to students
units.fit_note: Describes a deterrent benefit of presence at exams, not a shift of assessment weight.

units.why: Advises 'Use Empathy' when confronting a student and to frame the inquiry 'in terms of educational growth'; an educative, non-punitive response to suspected misuse (P68) rather than P57, which is talking before escalating.
units.anchor: Consider framing your initial inquiry in terms of educational growth

units.why: Notes students 'have reported increased stress regarding potential false or wrongful accusations'; a factual reason for empathy in handling suspicion, informs, closest P68 (reduce pressures, presume good faith).
units.anchor: Students have reported increased stress regarding potential false or wrongful accusations
units.fit_note: Gives evidence of student stress about false accusations rather than prescribing an educative response.

units.why: The sample script says 'Let's talk about how you arrived at these results', a conversation with the student about their work as the first step in handling suspicion; P57 (talk before escalating).
units.anchor: Let’s talk about how you arrived at these results/insights/conclusions.
units.fit_note: Gives a sample script for a conversation; escalation is not mentioned explicitly.

units.why: 'ask questions regarding the course content to assess if they understand' checks understanding by questioning the student in a meeting, which is P34.
units.anchor: ask questions regarding the course content to assess if they understand the course content
units.frag_start: During your meeting with the student

units.why: 'Not disclosing the information that led to your suspicion can often result in the student also hiding information' advises transparency toward the student; nearest P57 (context-gathering before escalating), with a fit note since it is about openness.
units.anchor: Addressing the issue with transparency about your suspicion can help
units.fit_note: Concerns instructors sharing the basis for suspicion with the student, closer to fairness and transparency than to pre-escalation conversation.

units.why: Instructors should 'ask to see versions from their drafting process'; using drafts as process evidence of misuse, P40.
units.anchor: ask to see versions from their drafting process
units.frag_start: Ask the student about their working methods
units.fit_note: Process evidence is requested from the student in a conversation, not from software or logs.

units.why: States AI detection tools 'are not completely reliable and have shown bias', and not to overstate their reliability; reliability caution on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: AI detection tools are not completely reliable and have shown bias
units.frag_start: AI detection tools are not completely
units.fit_note: Detectors are not banned; they may help point to identifiers but cannot be proof alone.

units.why: 'their results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused' sets an evidence standard for findings, so P69 rather than P39 (the standard of proof is the load-bearing element).
units.anchor: their results alone cannot constitute a preponderance of evidence that AI was misused
units.frag_start: While these tools can help point out

units.why: Advises checking citations because AI 'can generate wrong links or hallucinate citations' and ChatGPT leaves 'utm_source=chatgpt.com'; a way to identify misuse via artifacts in the work, P40.
units.anchor: ChatGPT leaves a remnant in the URL hyperlink in papers if ChatGPT was used
units.frag_start: Often, AI can generate wrong links
units.fit_note: Identification relies on AI-generated artifacts in the submitted text, not on software, commit history or logs.

units.why: Checking 'inconsistencies between a student's writing' can point to technology misuse, a way to identify misuse via evidence in the work; P40.
units.anchor: inconsistencies between a student’s writing, either in one assignment or multiple, can help point
units.fit_note: Stylistic comparison across submissions, not software or logs.

units.why: Warns to 'be cautious when confronting improvements in performance' since improvement is desirable; limits what counts as evidence of misuse, P69 (a hunch is not enough).
units.anchor: be cautious when confronting improvements in performance through a course

units.why: Suggests having students write 'completely in a Google Document' to view version history; process evidence from activity logs, P40.
units.anchor: write assignments completely in a Google Document can be a helpful way to view

units.why: Handwritten assignments 'can help to focus students' attention and reduce overreliance on electronic resources'; assignment format redesigned to limit AI reliance, P35.
units.anchor: can help to focus students’ attention and reduce overreliance on electronic resources
units.frag_start: whether in part or in full,

units.why: Invites faculty to 'consult with the Honor Committee' before or after talking with a student, and lists contacts; a support and referral channel that fits no type well.
units.anchor: feel free to consult with the Honor Committee!
units.frag_start: If you have questions, either before
units.uncovered_note: Instructors may consult the Faculty or Student Honor Committee or the Honor System Liaison for advice on suspected misuse.

notes: Single included document. Guidance addresses faculty; the Honor Code Charter itself was not collected.
